You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a

Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges

}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that

- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones

```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

prompt.content:
You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

prompt.content:
You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges

- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a

- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

prompt.content:
You are an interpretability researcher analyzing attribution graphs of a
language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

You are given the prompt tokens, the model's top output tokens, the graph's
nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

Group the FEATURE nodes into supernodes — clusters of features that represent
the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

Your proposal is verified CAUSALLY: each supernode you propose will be ablated
in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:
- Coverage: you are scored on the fraction of total feature influence your
  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

Rules:
- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit
  node ids.
- Each feature node belongs to at most one supernode; use 2-8 supernodes.
- Every supernode must have at least one outgoing edge — a group that
  affects nothing is not part of the circuit.
- "output" is a reserved terminal node: draw an edge ["<supernode>", "output"]
  from any supernode that directly drives the predicted token.
- Name supernodes by their concept (e.g. "Texas", "say a capital", "ones
  digit is 5").

Respond with a short analysis, then a single JSON code block:
```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```

language model (Qwen3-4B) computed with per-layer transcoders, following
Anthropic's "Circuit Tracing" methodology.

nodes (transcoder features, embedding and logit nodes) and the strongest
edges (direct linear attributions).

the same concept and play the same causal role — and describe the circuit as
directed edges between supernodes.

in the actual model (features clamped to 0), and the measured effects must
propagate exactly along your edges — ablating a supernode should strongly
reduce the supernodes and output it can reach through your edges, and leave
unreachable supernodes untouched. Both missing edges and superfluous edges
cost you. Additionally:

  supernodes capture, so include every feature that matters.
- Completeness: all features you leave ungrouped are ablated together — if
  that shifts the predicted token, your circuit missed something.
- Balance: no single supernode may hold most of the grouped influence; a
  catch-all blob scores zero.

- Supernode members must be FEATURE node ids only — never embedding or logit

  digit is 5").

```json
{
  "supernodes": [{"name": "<concept>", "nodes": ["<node_id>", ...]}, ...],
  "edges": [["<source supernode>", "<target supernode or output>"], ...]
}
```
